clue.text: Sore second rate celebrity (7)

blocks.note: the fluid-filled bubble a new shoe rubs up on a heel
the papers rank fame in lists, and the second of them holds the lesser names

annotation.surface: A minor famous face nursing a grievance.
annotation.walkthrough: The same seven letters read two ways, and the second reading wants a hyphen the clue never prints. 'Sore' is the trap: the sentence offers it as a mood, and the definition needs the noun on your foot.
annotation.definitionFit: A blister is the raised sore rubbing produces on skin; and a B-lister is a celebrity from fame's second rank rather than the first.

clue.text: Starts to bitch about failure to achieve such awards (6)

indicators.note: What a word starts to be is its opening letter, so only the first letter of each word that follows is taken.

blocks.clueFragment: bitch about failure to achieve such
blocks.note: the opening letters of these six words, read in order

annotation.surface: Grumbling about never having managed something.
annotation.walkthrough: BAFTA is the British Academy of Film and Television Arts, whose statuettes are Britain's answer to the Oscars. Six short words in a row of complaint hide the initials, and 'such' is there to supply the last one.
annotation.definitionFit: The BAFTAs are the annual prizes handed out by the British Academy of Film and Television Arts, so the plural names a set of awards.

clue.text: Hot Italian leader? Bring it on! (6)

definitions.note: The verb being defined is 'bring on'; the setter drops 'it' between the two halves so the surface can end as a challenge.

blocks.note: what is in is what is hot this season
il Duce was Mussolini's title, from the Italian word for leader

annotation.surface: Someone relishing the prospect of a good-looking Italian boss.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hot' is doing the fashion job rather than the temperature one. The Italian leader is Mussolini, and the question mark admits he is one instance of the breed rather than the word's meaning.
annotation.definitionFit: To induce something is to bring it on: doctors induce labour and a shock induces panic, both of them things brought about deliberately.

clue.text: Heated Tory upset from first moment (3,4,3)

indicators.note: Something upset has been knocked out of the arrangement it was in, so these letters are re-sorted rather than read as they stand.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, filling all three words of the answer

annotation.surface: An angry Conservative knocked off balance right from the start.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The year dot' is British for the very beginning of time, heard almost always in 'since the year dot', the dot being the nought of a date nobody wrote down. 'Upset' reads as the politician's temper.
annotation.definitionFit: The year dot is the earliest date there could be, the point everything is reckoned from, so it names the first moment of all.

clue.text: Fourth line has yankee being disorderly (5)

blocks.note: lines of seats are lettered from A, so the fourth line is row D
yankee is Y in the radio alphabet

annotation.surface: An American misbehaving in the fourth row of seats.
annotation.walkthrough: Yankee is the radio alphabet's letter here, not an American, and that is the one convention the clue turns on. 'Being disorderly' is the charge sheet's own phrase, which is what lets the definition sit at the end unnoticed.
annotation.definitionFit: Rowdy means noisy and unruly — the rowdy element at a match — which is what being disorderly describes.

clue.text: Standard way to cut vegetable (7)

blocks.note: par is the standard score set for a golf hole
a snip of the scissors is one way of cutting

annotation.surface: The usual method of chopping up a vegetable.
annotation.walkthrough: Par is golf's standard, and the sentence reads as kitchen advice from end to end, so nothing in it announces itself as wordplay. The definition is the last word, which the surface also needs as its object.
annotation.definitionFit: A parsnip is the pale tapering root vegetable roasted alongside the potatoes at Sunday lunch.

clue.text: Stick with training run that’s very tough (9)

blocks.note: PE is physical education, the school timetable's physical training
r = run, the abbreviation off a cricket scorecard
a severe test is a very tough one

annotation.surface: Sticking with a punishing training run.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole sentence is one picture of hard training, which hides the join between the definition and the three pieces. 'Run' looks like the exercise and is a single letter off a cricket scorecard.
annotation.definitionFit: To persevere is to keep at something that is not going well, which is what sticking with it amounts to.

clue.text: Something written up in birthday card is risque (4)

indicators.note: In a down entry what is written up runs from the bottom towards the top, so the letters are read backwards.
What is in a phrase lies inside it, so the letters wanted sit unbroken within the words that follow.

blocks.note: the last letter of birthday and the first three of card give YCAR, read back up the entry

annotation.surface: The message inside a birthday card turning out to be near the knuckle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Written up' can only mean backwards in a down entry, and the words really do hold a message written in a card. Risqué is the mild sort of rude, the joke that just gets away with it.
annotation.definitionFit: Racy means suggestive without being obscene — a racy anecdote — which is the sense of risqué the clue prints without its accent.

clue.text: Note ruin that’s been rebuilt – it’s very very small (8)

definitions.note: The answer is a noun and the definition a description of one: the setter names the particle by the single property everybody has heard about it.

indicators.note: What has been rebuilt was taken down first and put up in a new arrangement, so these letters go back together in another order.

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder

annotation.surface: A restored ruin that turns out to be disappointingly tiny.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Note' reads as an instruction to the reader and is the first four letters of the raw material. Neutrinos stream through the earth by the trillion without touching anything, which is the 'very very' the definition leans on.
annotation.definitionFit: A neutrino is the almost massless particle that passes straight through matter, so the description is plain fact about it rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Sick types tucking tie into trousers (8)

indicators.note: To tuck a thing away is to push it out of sight inside something else, which is where the letters named next go.
Into names the destination, so those letters finish up within the word that follows rather than beside it.

blocks.note: pants are trousers in American usage
the clue's own word goes in whole

annotation.surface: Somebody tucking a necktie down inside their trousers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sick types' looks like a comment on whoever dresses that way, and it is the definition. Pants are trousers only in the American sense; the British underwear reading leaves the tie nowhere sensible to go.
annotation.definitionFit: Patients are the people under a doctor's care, which is how a hospital counts the sick, the word sharing its root with patience.

clue.text: Avoid making something explicit or sweet (5)

blocks.note: what a politician does to a question they will not answer straight
the soft block of boiled sugar, butter and milk sold in slabs

annotation.surface: Advice to keep away from anything too explicit or too sugary.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Or' works as an equals sign rather than a choice, which is how two definitions sit in one sentence. To fudge an issue is to blur it on purpose, while the confectionery reading has no metaphor in it at all.
annotation.definitionFit: To fudge a question is to answer so vaguely that nothing is made explicit; and fudge is also the slab of boiled sugar sold in seaside shops.

clue.text: Amount written about matter on news (4,5)

indicators.note: In an across answer a thing laid on another has been put down after it, so the piece before 'on' follows the piece after it.

blocks.note: word of an event is news of it, as in word came through
what counts is what matters

annotation.surface: The length of a piece written about a current story.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'concerning' and does nothing but join the halves. 'Matter' is the verb — what matters counts — rather than the substance the sentence seems to be describing.
annotation.definitionFit: A word count is how many words a piece runs to, the amount written measured the way an editor measures it.

clue.text: Models spy cheater getting messy (10)

indicators.note: Something getting messy is losing the order it was in, so these letters are to be shuffled into another.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder

annotation.surface: Fashion models spotting a cheat as the scene turns ugly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Models' reads as the people on the catwalk and wants the other sense, the pattern other things are copied from. 'Spy' is a verb in the surface and raw material in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: An archetype is the original pattern a whole class of things is copied from, so archetypes are models in the sense of templates rather than mannequins.

clue.text: English town that makes whiskey for America (3)

blocks.note: the cobbled hill town in East Sussex, once a Cinque Port and now a mile from the sea
the American spirit distilled from the grain of that name

annotation.surface: An English town with a distillery selling to America.
annotation.walkthrough: The e in 'whiskey' is the flag for America: American and Irish distillers keep it where Scotch drops it. The town and the grain share a name and nothing else, which is the whole of the joke.
annotation.definitionFit: Rye is a small town in East Sussex; and rye is the American whiskey distilled from that grain, spelt with the e the clue is careful to print.

clue.text: Travel like fugitives? (4,6)

definitions.note: The second half defines by example rather than by synonym, saying what fugitives do instead of giving a verb, which is what the question mark owns up to.

blocks.note: to leave the ground and go, flight being the word the airlines print on the ticket
to run for it, which is what somebody on the run does

annotation.surface: Getting away the way people on the run get away.
annotation.walkthrough: Two senses of flight are at work: the one you book and the one you make when the police are behind you. The question mark is load-bearing, since fugitives are an example rather than a meaning.
annotation.definitionFit: To take flight is to leave the ground and travel through the air; and it is equally what fugitives do when they flee.

clue.text: Gifted German fabricated cooler decoration (6,6)

indicators.note: What is fabricated has been made up out of whatever parts were to hand, so these letters are built into something new.

blocks.note: twelve letters of fodder, filling both words

annotation.surface: A talented German inventing a piece of ornament.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cooler' is the kitchen appliance, not a prison or a coolbox, and the decoration is the souvenir stuck on its door. Twelve letters of fodder fill the grid exactly, which is worth counting before trusting a long anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: A fridge magnet is the small souvenir clamped to the front of a fridge, decoration for the household cooler.

clue.text: Concerning evolution of a wind / rain formation (9)

indicators.note: A formation is parts arranged into a shape, so the letters in front are put into a new order.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, the slash only punctuation between the two kinds of weather

annotation.surface: How a weather formation of wind and rain comes about.
annotation.walkthrough: The adjective wanted is the one made from the surname of the naturalist who proposed natural selection. 'Formation' looks like the thing the weather is doing and is the instruction instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Darwinian means belonging to Darwin's account of evolution by natural selection, so it is the adjective for anything concerning evolution in that sense.

clue.text: Deposits required to get somewhere to live (8)

definitions.note: Lodgings is plural in form but names one rented place, which is why the second definition is singular.

blocks.note: to lodge money or a document is to deposit it for safe keeping
rented rooms in somebody else's house, the older word for digs

annotation.surface: The money a landlord wants up front before handing over keys.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves come off the same verb, which is what lets the sentence read as one thought about renting. To lodge a sum with a bank is to deposit it; to lodge with a landlady is to take her spare room.
annotation.definitionFit: Things lodged for safe keeping are deposits; and lodgings are equally the rented rooms a lodger lives in.

clue.text: Countdown starting at 12.50? (3,2,3)

definitions.note: The first half describes rather than substitutes: a countdown is the run of numbers the answer names, which is what the question mark concedes.

blocks.note: the numbers called out before a launch, from the top one down to the last
ten minutes before one o'clock, said the way anyone says the time

annotation.surface: A launch countdown beginning at ten to one in the afternoon.
annotation.walkthrough: The full stop in 12.50 is the British way of writing a time, and the clue wants it spoken rather than read as a number. A countdown covers the same three words going the other way.
annotation.definitionFit: A countdown runs ten to one before the off; and 12.50 is ten minutes to one on the clock.

clue.text: Points achieved from All Black clearance (3,4,5)

definitions.text: Points achieved from All Black clearance

blocks.note: read as one of New Zealand's rugby players, and meant as every red taken with the black
read as a kick downfield out of defence, and meant as potting every ball on the table in one visit
read as a score run up in a match, and meant as a break total written out in words

annotation.surface: A rugby side running up points from a clearance kick.
annotation.walkthrough: 147 is the maximum break in snooker: fifteen reds each followed by the black, then the six colours in order. The capital letters buy the New Zealand rugby side, who score points of a quite different size.
annotation.definitionFit: One four seven is the highest break a snooker player can make, the points that come from taking the black after every red and then clearing the colours.

clue.text: Old king appealing to have article suppressed (6)

indicators.note: To suppress a thing is to hold it down out of sight, so the letters named go buried inside the word before them.

blocks.note: cute is appealing in the winsome sense
an is one of the indefinite articles, not an abbreviation of anything

annotation.surface: A charming old monarch getting a newspaper piece hushed up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Article' is the grammar sense, not the newspaper one the rest of the sentence sets up. Canute is the Dane who ruled England a thousand years ago, remembered for having his throne carried to the tide to prove he could not command it.
annotation.definitionFit: Canute ruled England, Denmark and Norway in the eleventh century, which makes him an old king in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Times worker not using machinery (2,4)

blocks.note: three times four is three by four, the multiplication read aloud
a hand is a hired worker, as on a farm or a ship

annotation.surface: A newspaper employee doing without machines.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Times' is capitalised to sell the newspaper and means multiplied by. The hand is the farm or deck worker, the sense still heard in 'all hands on deck'.
annotation.definitionFit: Work done by hand is done with the hands alone, the phrase a label uses to promise no machinery was involved.

clue.text: Obtained heroin from old German (3)

indicators.note: Taking one thing from another leaves the remainder, so the letter named is struck out of the word that follows.

blocks.note: the Goths were the Germanic people who overran the Roman empire
h = heroin in the dealer's shorthand, and it is the letter taken away

annotation.surface: Scoring drugs off an elderly German.
annotation.walkthrough: The old German is a Goth rather than a pensioner from Munich, and the drug is one letter rather than a substance. 'Obtained' is past tense, and so is what the deletion leaves.
annotation.definitionFit: Got is the past of get, and to get a thing is to come by it, so both words report an acquisition already made.

clue.text: Slam nicely arranged assortment (10)

indicators.note: Things arranged have been put into an order somebody chose, so these letters go into another order too.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder

annotation.surface: Panning a collection that somebody had laid out with care.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Slam' is the review page's verb in the surface and raw material in the wordplay, while 'nicely arranged' sounds like praise for the display. A miscellany is usually a book: pieces gathered with nothing in common but the covers.
annotation.definitionFit: A miscellany is a collection of unrelated items brought together, which is what an assortment is.

clue.text: Business leader receives a million for brief appearance (5)

indicators.note: Somebody who receives a thing takes it in, so the letters that follow go inside the word before.

blocks.note: the chief executive officer leads the business
the clue's own word goes in as it stands
m = million, as in a salary printed £2m

annotation.surface: A company boss taking a million-pound payment.
annotation.walkthrough: The money reads as one sum and splits into two pieces, the little word and the abbreviation the papers set against a figure. A cameo was first a small carved portrait, which is where the walk-on part got its name.
annotation.definitionFit: A cameo is a brief appearance by a well-known actor in someone else's film, a part measured in seconds.

clue.text: Extravagant dressers finally off to pop-up shops (4)

indicators.note: What comes finally comes at the very end, so only the closing letter of each word that follows is taken.

blocks.note: the last letters of off, to, pop-up and shops in order

annotation.surface: Flashy dressers heading out to the temporary shops.
annotation.walkthrough: The hyphen keeps pop-up as a single word, so it gives up one letter rather than two. A fop is the eighteenth-century dandy whose whole occupation was his clothes.
annotation.definitionFit: A fop is a man absurdly taken up with his own clothes, so fops are extravagant dressers in the vain rather than the costly sense.

clue.text: Coinage may prompt solvers to say ‘never heard of it’ (9)

definitions.text: Coinage may prompt solvers to say ‘never heard of it’

blocks.note: read as money struck at the mint, and meant as a word somebody has just minted

blocks.clueFragment: may prompt solvers to say ‘never heard of it’
blocks.note: read as a complaint about an unfair answer, and meant as plain truth about a word too new for anybody's dictionary

annotation.surface: Solvers protesting that the answer is a word nobody has ever used.
annotation.walkthrough: There is nothing here to take apart into letters: the clue turns on coinage meaning a minted word as readily as minted money. The joke is aimed at the solver, because a brand-new word is precisely the one you could not have heard of.
annotation.definitionFit: A neologism is a newly coined word, a coinage in the language sense, and being new it is one nobody has heard before.

clue.text: Leave tundra regularly to find cheese (5)

indicators.note: Taken regularly means taken at a steady interval, so every other letter of the word before is picked out.

blocks.note: to go is to leave
the second, fourth and sixth letters of tundra

annotation.surface: Someone obliged to leave the tundra now and then to get cheese.
annotation.walkthrough: Even letters are wanted rather than odd ones, and 'regularly' leaves that open until you try both. Gouda is the Dutch town near Rotterdam where the cheese was traded.
annotation.definitionFit: Gouda is the mild yellow Dutch cheese sold in flat wheels under a wax rind, named after the town that marketed it.

clue.text: Crushes relative (7)

definitions.note: The first definition works on the answer respaced as two words, a verb phrase for treading something flat, while the entry itself is a noun.

blocks.note: crushing something underfoot is stepping on it
the son your husband or wife had before you married

annotation.surface: A headline about somebody crushing a member of the family.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words and seven letters are all there is, and one of them wants the answer respaced. 'Crushes' is the foot sense, treading something flat, rather than the infatuation the word usually carries now.
annotation.definitionFit: To step on something is to crush it underfoot; and a stepson is the son a husband or wife brought to the marriage.

clue.text: In central Bonn district, French cider is fashionable (2,5)

indicators.note: What is in the centre of a word is the letter or two at its very middle, so each word that follows gives up only its heart.

blocks.note: the middle two of its four letters
the middle two of its eight letters
the middle two of its six letters
the middle one of its five letters

annotation.surface: French cider selling well in the middle of Bonn.
annotation.walkthrough: Four words in a row each give up their middles, two letters from the even ones and a single letter from the odd one. 'Central' reads as the city centre, and the commas are there only to keep the sentence plausible.
annotation.definitionFit: Something on trend is in line with the fashion of the moment, the phrase the style pages use where they once said in vogue.
